content.title: About
content.content: Ham is cured or smoked pork meat, typically taken from the hind leg (the ham). It is traditionally prepared by salting, aging, and often smoking, which gives it a distinctive flavor and extends its shelf life. Ham is widely used in sandwiches, salads, appetizers, and cooked dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Ham production dates back to ancient Rome, where it was known as "perna".
There are more than 30 varieties of ham, including Parma, Prosciutto, city‑style ham, and smoked ham.
Traditional Italian Parma ham is aged for a minimum of 12 months, sometimes up to 3 years.
Ham can be smoked cold (below 30 °C) or hot (up to 80 °C), affecting its taste and texture.
Ham is a staple in holiday meals, such as Christmas casseroles and the American "ham‑glazed" dishes.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Ham provides about 20 g of protein per 100 g, supporting muscle maintenance.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Ham supplies B1, B3, and B12 vitamins, essential for energy metabolism and nervous system health.

items.title: Zinc
items.content: Zinc in ham supports immune function and wound healing.

items.title: Iron
items.content: Iron contributes to normal hemoglobin levels.

items.title: Selenium
items.content: Selenium has antioxidant properties and aids thyroid function.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Ham often contains 800–1500 mg of sodium per 100 g, which can raise blood pressure.

items.title: Nitrates and nitrites
items.content: These preservatives are used to maintain color and prevent bacterial growth, but long‑term consumption may form potentially harmful compounds.

items.title: Saturated fats
items.content: Ham contains saturated fats, so individuals with high cholesterol should limit intake.

items.title: Pork allergy
items.content: Some people may have an allergy or intolerance to pork.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Ham can be sliced thin for sandwiches, added to salads, used in casseroles, omelets, and pasta dishes. It is also often served hot, glazed with brown sugar or pineapple.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store ham in the refrigerator at 0–4 °C in its original packaging or an airtight container. Fresh smoked ham lasts up to 1 week, while cooked ham lasts up to 2 weeks. For longer storage, freeze it in a sealed bag for up to 3 months. Before use, check for off‑odors or discoloration; discard if any signs of spoilage are present.
